The central and southern coastal plain soils are
similar to those of the northern plain, but are mainly
covered by sandy detritus which supports only pine
forest and dry savannah. The riverine alluvial belts
support a rich rain forest, characterised by the pres-
ence of cohune palm. These soils, derived from the
igneous rocks of the central mass, are deeper and
more fertile than those of the northern plain, although
more acidic. The valleys and lower hill slopes of the
central mountain region contain a deep red fertile soil
in granitic areas; this soil becomes shallower in slate,
schist and quartzite areas.
The southern Toledo region has deep fertile soils in
the well-drained areas, but much of the land consists
of heavy water-logged clays.
The Mayan Indians are known to have cultivated
large areas of Belize between 300 B.C. and 900 A.D.,
growing such crops as maize, beans, cassava and
coco. Terraces remaining from this civilisation are
still visible on limestone hills in the Chiquibul area of
Cayo District. Present-day Mayan farmers still oper-
ate the milpa system of their ancestors, whereby
annual slashing and burning of new tracts of forest is
undertaken. This shifting agriculture has been res-
ponsible for the clearance of forest from large tracts
of land.
Early British settlers and African slaves realised
the potential of logwood (Haematoxylon campechia-
nuт L.) for dyes and mahogany for timber, and by
1850, Belize City had developed as a trading port.
Mexican Cedar (Cedrela mexicana M.J. Roem) and
rosewood (Dalbergia stevensonii Standley) were the
other important timbers found in the hinterland.
The establishment of British Honduras as a crown
colony in 1862 saw the development of large agricul-
tural estates, with cane being planted in Toledo and
the northern districts for sugar and rum production.
With the riverine system being the virtual sole means
of transport, poor communications into the interior
did much to lessen the economic prosperity. In the
late 1890's, cattle production increased in Cayo and
the northern districts following the importation of
Guinea grass (Panicum maxiтum Nees) and Pará
grass (Panicum purpurescens Opiz). By 1900
Creole-populated riverside and Carib-populated
coastal smallholdings were established, growing
corn, bananas and plantains. Coconuts have always
been important, particularly in the first quarter of this
century. In 1937, sigatoka leaf spot and Panama dis-
ease of bananas caused a decline in that industry,
forcing farmers to expand citrus, especially orange
and grapefruit, production in the Stann Creek Valley.
Introduction
Small areas of rice production have been developed
in Belize and Toledo Districts.
Clearance of land in the northern districts for the
production of sugar and cattle has resulted in a se-
rious loss of orchid habitat, particularly in Corozal.
Likewise, removal of logwood and other timbers has
taken its toll of epiphytic orchid habitat in logwood
stands and rain forest. Citrus plantations, which are
particularly resistant to permanent damage by hurri-
canes, have, however, produced a micro-environ-
ment suitable for many epiphytic species. Indeed
some species, such as Psygmorchis pusilla (L.) Dod-
son & Dressler, are rarely found outside of grapefruit
groves. Catling, Brownell & Lefkovitch (1986) and
Catling & Catling (1987) have carried out some
interesting ecological studies of epiphytic orchids in
a Belizean grapefruit orchard.
Over the last 15 years, Belize has witnessed a
relatively large influx of refugees from the civil war
in El Salvador. The majority of these were milpa
farmers, with a resultant ribbon development along-
side roads and rivers, particularly in Cayo and Stann
Creek Districts. This practice has led to further orchid
habitat loss.
The Government of Belize, in efforts to safeguard
the environment, has ensured the protection of over
30 reserves and parks, ranging from as little as 8
hectares, to over 107,000 hectares in the case of the
Chiquibul National Park. When declared as a pro-
tected area under the National Park System Act of
1981, activities such as felling, burning, injuring or
removing any trees, squatting, grazing or pasturing of
cattle, hunting, shooting and fishing are prohibited
In other areas, licences and permits are issued
under Belize's Forest Act for controlling forestry, to
ensure sustained utilisation by monitoring of the re-
sources.
This bodes well for the future of the native orchid
species in Belize, and the People and Government
must be congratulated for their attempts to link con-
servation with development.
1.2 VEGETATION
Northern Belize has a similar flora to that of the
Mexican part of the Yucatán Peninsula, while the
central mountains, with the exception of some
limestone hilltops, and Toledo District have more in
common botanically with Guatemala. Many of the
plants found in Belize are widely distributed along
the Atlantic slope from Mexico to northern South
America. However, a considerable number are

form a marginal forest along streams, where the soil
is somewhat richer. Shrubs are rare in the open pine-
land, but the orchids Cattleya bowringiana O'Brien,
with its attractive purple flowers, and Encyclia beli-
zensis (Rchb. f.) Schltr. ssp. belizensis are locally
common on rocky outcrops, whereas Sobralia mac-
rantha Lindl., with its short-lasting flowers, is seen
growing in clumps among the grasses, sedges and
legumes of the herbaceous ground cover.
The vegetation along the streams and upland
marshes consists of small shrubs and trees, alternated
with marsh and rocky areas. Steep grassy banks and
dense palmetto palms add to the variety. Of the trees,
Clusia spp. dominate, with scattered pines and Billy
Webb (Sweetia panamensis Benth.), along with
pockets of the teabox shrub (Myrica cerifera L.). The
vegetation bordering these streams undoubtedly
offers the richest variety of Belizean epiphytic
orchids, particularly Maxillaria species. The larger
streams along the western edge of the Mountain Pine
Ridge are liable to become torrents after heavy rains,
but they equally rapidly subside. Here the vegetation
is similar, but is interspersed with areas of tall rain
forest growing on the rich black alluvia of the flood
plain. Clumps of the tree fern (Sphaeropteris myosu-
roides (Liebm.) Tryon) occur in densely shaded val-
leys. Cattleya bowringiana and Encyclia belizensis
subsp. belizensis are again locally common, with the
rarer Encyclia alata (Batem.) Schltr., growing along
river banks, particularly of the Rio On. A belt of
marginal forest consisting of scattered pines, oaks
and silver pimentos with an undercover of shrubs and
herbs exists between the pines and the rain forest on
open rocky banks of the larger streams. The forest of
the limestone borderland contains pines and oaks, but
the undergrowth gives way to lime-loving species
such as the abundant bayleaf palm (Sabal mayarum
H.H. Bartlett).
The forest of the bordering limestone hills contains
many species typical of the dry deciduous forest of
the northern part of the Yucatán Peninsula, such as
manzanilla (Coccoloba cozumelensis Hemsl.) and
redwood (Erythroxylon areolatum L.). Many of the
species are found in the wooded swamps of southern
Campeche in Mexico, and the adjoining Department
of Petén, Guatemala, and are significant in interpreta-
tion of the vegetation of the peninsula. These species
are among those dominating the cactus thicket and
deciduous forest of Yucatán and Quintana Roo, Me-
xico. Their presence as relics on dry hills in the much
higher rainfall southern areas of Belize may indicate
that the climate was considerably drier or that Mayan
clearances favoured growth of these plants. This
Introduction
vegetation on the tops of the limestone hills suggests
that cactus thicket and deciduous forests were more
extensive than now. Coelia bella (Lem.) Rchb. f. and
several species of Epidendrum are among the many
orchids which may be found in these areas.
The intermediate rain forest occupies the niche
between swamp or pine forest and advanced rain
forest. Common tree species include mahogany, al-
though much has now been removed, Santa María,
Billy Webb, negrito (Simarouba amara Aubl.), cher-
ry (Pseudolmedia spuria Griseb.) and madre de
cacao (Gliricidia sepium (Jacq.) Kunth. ex Walp.).
Three associations of this so-called 'broken ridge' are
apparent. In the north, swamp and pine forests give
way to bayleaf palm, give-and-take palm (Cryoso-
phila argentea H.H. Bartlett), sapodilla and silly
young (Pouteria amygdalina (Standley) Baehni); the
dry pine forest of the central region is colonised by
whitemalady (Aspidospermastegomeris (R.E.
Woodson) R.E. Woodson), pigeon plum (Licania
hypoleuca Benth.), carbón (Hedwigia panamensis
Engl.), introduced mountain cabbage palm (Euterpe
oleracea Engel) and tree fern, whereas in the central
and Toledo regions,swamp and savannah forests
give way to nargusta (Terminalia amazonia (J.F
Gmel.) Exell), Santa María, waika chewstick and
yemeri (Vochysia hondurensis Sprague).
Mountain rain forest on ridges of high elevation in
the central region is an intermediate between the
mountain pine and advanced forest of the lower
slopes. Since these mountains are remains of meta-
morphic rocks intruded into the older limestones
which are now almost eroded, it is remarkable that
this region has similar species to the savannahs i.e.
waika chewstick, Santa María, swamp fig and Pur-
diaea belizensis, as well as mountain cabbage palm
and species of oak.
Advanced rain forest is characterised by the
cohune palm, which often forms a dense sub-canopy,
and undergrowth which ousts dicotyledonous spe-
cies. Several species of tall trees are found, along
with abundant shrubs which are replaced in the den-
ser forest by palms or small ferns. Epiphytes abound,
particularly orchids, bromeliads, aroids, ferns and
mosses. Tree species include the tall spreading
cotton-tree (Ceiba pentandra (L.) Gaertn.), Santa
María, nargusta, yemeri, mamee apple (Pouteria
mammosa (L.) Cronquist), prickly yellow (Zanthoxy-
lum kellermanii P. Wilson), hog plum (Spondias
mombin L.), rubber (Castilla elastica Cerv.) and figs.
Cedar and breadnut (Brosimum alicastrum Sw.) are
found only on calcareous soils.
The Maya cultivated large areas of rain forest,
leaving the cohune palm for shade and oil. This

lines.text: GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize and Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Exact locality not
known. Rare.
HABITAT. In elfin forests.
FLOWERING SEASON. October.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin erosus (having an
irregularly toothed margin).
NoTE. Reported by Siegerist (1984) but not seen
by us.
Terrestrial or semi-epiphytic herbs, relatively small,
arising from a creeping rhizome. Stems erect, sheath-
ed by bracts or the bases of petiolate leaves. Leaves
with short petioles that surround the base of the stem,
usually reticulate-veined. Inflorescence a terminal
raceme. Flowers very small, fleshy. Dorsal sepal and
petals arch over the lip; lateral sepals are free. Lip
3-lobed, with the base dilated into a prominent sack-
like spur; rostellum entire, flat, elliptic to suborbicu-
lar, sometimes emarginate.
There are more than 100 species distributed in the
American tropics and subtropics. Two are known
from Belize.
L.A. Garay (1977) transferred some species of
Erythrodes to the new genus Platythelys on the basis
that Erythrodes,astypifiedbythe type species E
latifolia Blume, has an erect, bipartite, clearly
defined rostellum with tapering segments after the
viscidium has been removed while the rostellum of
Platythelys is different. It is entire, flat, elliptic to
suborbicular, its tip is commonly ruptured by the
removal of the viscidium, rarely, it appears to be
emarginate. Moreover, the tiny flowers are very
fleshy.
ETYMoLoGY: From the Greek platys (flat) and
thelys (pertaining to a woman) in reference to the
broad flat rostellum.
Leaves ovate-lanceolate; inflorescence sessile, usual-
ly densely flowered....
Leaves lanceolate-linear; inflorescence subsessile,
often loosely flowered...

Plants terrestrial with slightly hairy roots. Leaves
basal, several and petiolate. Scape slender, erect and
bracteolate. Inflorescences terminal, densely many-
flowered, spicate. Flowers very small. Sepals free,
occasionally connate; lateral sepals with a subdecur-
rent base. Petals parallel. Lip unguiculate, claw ad-
nate to the base of the lateral sepals. Column short
with an inflated clinandrium.
Seven species are native to the American tropics
and subtropics. One is known from Belize.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek belos (a dart) and
glossa (a tongue) in reference to the shape of the lip
of the type species, Spiranthes costaricensis (Rchb.

Beloglottis costaricensis (Rchb.f.) Schltr. in Beih.
Bot. Centralbl. 37 (2): 364 (1920). Type: Costa Rica,
Öersted (holo. W!).
Spiranthes costaricensis Rchb.f. in Bonplandia 3:
S. bicaudata Ames, Orchid., 7: 126 (1922).
Plant terrestrial, slender, up to 40 cm tall. Scape
almost concealed by tubular-acuminate bracts. Lea-
ves basal, elliptic-oblong, acute, tapering at base, up
to 19 cm long and 6 cm wide; petioles narrow.
Inflorescence spicate, racemose or compact. Flowers
green or white, tubular, flaring at apex, strongly fra-
grant of violets. Sepals slightly hairy on outer sur-
face, up to 7 mm long and 1.5 mm wide; lateral sepals
united for a short distance at base forming a sack,
linear-lanceolate; dorsal sepal linear, concave at base.
Petals linear, recurved at apex. Lip with a broad claw,
triangular-ovate, apex ciliate, up to 6 mm long. Col-
umn short, up to 3 mm long, bristly on anterior
surface. (Fig. 4).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Me-
xico and Central America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District.
HABITAT. In moist mixed forest, on slopes or
along roadsides.
FLOWERING SEASON. February and March.
EtymoLogY. From Costa Rica, and the Latin ad-
jectival suffix -ensis, referring to the country of origin
of the type specimen.
Small to medium-sized terrestrial or epiphytic herbs
with fleshy, fasciculate roots. Leaves basal, in
rosettes, petiolate, lacking prominent venation. Sca-
pe slender, several-sheathed. Inflorescence spicate,
laxly to many-flowered. Flowers small, membrana-
ceous, pubescent on outer surface. Sepals similar,
basally connate forming a cylindrical tube, free
above with spreading segments. Petals connivent
with dorsal sepal. Lip broadly auriculate, the claw
free from the sepaline tube. Column free, elongate;
rostellum acute, bifid; pollinia 2, deeply-divided, cla-
vate.
There are about 70 species recorded from Florida,
the West Indies, Central and South America. Four are
known from Belize.
EtyMoLogY. From the Greek kyklos (a circle) and
pogon (a tail of fire with divided ends, bearded) in
reference to the sepals (reddish in dry condition)
which emerge from the circular sepaline tube.

Plant usually epiphytic, small, up to 16 cm tall when
in flower but often less. Leaves 3 to 5 in a basal
rosette, arising from a few fleshy swollen roots, lan-
ceolate, dark green, glossy, becoming pinkish-red
with prominent green veins when old, up to 7 cm long
and 2 cm wide, with a short petiole. Inflorescence
spicate, many-flowered, solitary, somewhat longer
than the leaves, slightly pubescent. Flowers greenish
or purplish-green with a white lip, subtended by a
large lanceolate bract, not fragrant, up to 1.4 cm long
including the pedicellate ovary. Dorsal sepal lanceo-
late, up to 6 mm long and 2 mm wide; lateral sepals
similar but up to 8 mm long and 2mm wide. Petals
linear, up to 5 mm long and 1 mm wide. Lip cons-
tricted above the middle, up to 6.5 mm long. Column
up to 4 mm long. (Photo. 16).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Rare.
HABITAT. Epiphytic or terrestrial in dense moist
forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. January and February.
ETYMOLOGY. From the Greek prasos (leek-green)
and phyllon (a leaf) referring to the colour of the
leaves.
Plants small to miniature, facultative epiphytes. Lea-
ves basal, rosulate with ciliate blades. Scape short,
erect. Inflorescences terminal, a densely compact,
capitate spike. Flowers very small, hidden by cilio-
late bracts. Sepals basally connate forming a tube;
dorsal sepal with a decurrent base, partially adnate to
the column; lateral sepals connate at base forming a
sac. Petals decurrent at base. Lip canaliculate, paral-
lel with column, broadly unguiculate. Column
slender with a long decurrent incurved foot.
A genus of about 13 species native to the American
tropics and subtropics. One is known from Belize.
ETYMOLOGY. From the Greek eurys (broad) and
stylis (a pillar or column) describing the shape of the
column which, in the original material unfortunately
was deformed.

Plant epiphytic, small, up to 3 cm tall. Stems absent or
reduced; roots white, fleshy. Leaves basal, up to 6 in a
rosette, elliptic, vernicose when living, margins un-
dulate, glossy, up to 27 mm long and 16 mm wide.
Inflorescence terminal, pendent; peduncle slender,
white-ciliate, head of flowers up to 1.5 cm long.
Flowers up to 25, often fewer, white tinged with
green, not fragrant, sessile, up to 6 mm long, not
opening widely; bracts pubescent, up to 1 cm long.

and 1 mm wide. Petals free, up to 3.5 mm long and 1
mm wide. Lip spathulate, 3-lobed at apex. Column up
to 4.5 mm long. (Fig. 6; Photo. 17).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Central America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees, especially vertical trunks, in
dense wet forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. December and January.
Flowers last about ten days.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin borealis (northern).
Plants terrestrial, small, commonly aphyllous during
anthesis. Roots fleshy, pubescent. Stems slender,
erect. Leaves small when present. Inflorescences ter-
minal, a spirally twisted spike. Flowers small. Sepals

concave; lateral sepals spreading. Petals variable. Lip
menbranaceous, panduriform with a short claw. Col-
umn short, dilated above, basally produced in a short
foot.
A genus of three species native to Mexico, Belize,
Trinidad, Venezuela, Bolivia and Brazil. One is
known from Belize.

characteristic for all species.

Plant terrestrial, short, stout with thick roots. Leaves
2 or more, basal. Stem puberulent, slender, up to 25
cm long. Leaves elliptic-oblanceolate, glabrous, thin,
petiolate, up to 12 cm long and 5 cm wide. Inflores-
cence a loosely flowered spike of 10-20 flowers,
subtended by lanceolate bracts. Flowers small, white
tinged with green-yellow, cystoliths present. Dorsal
sepal lanceolate, up to 4 mm long and 1.5 mm wide.
Lateral sepals linear- oblong, acute, up to 6 mm long.
Petals adnate to dorsal sepal, oblanceolate, up to 4
mm long and 1.2 mm wide. Lip oblanceolate, up to
5.5 mm long and 1.2 mm wide. Column up to 2 mm
long. (Fig. 8; Photo. 19).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize and Guatemala.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District.
HABITAT. Remnant rainforest in soil over lime-
stone rock.
FLOWERING SEASON. Not known.
ETymoLoGY. From Petén in Guatemala and the
Latin suffix -ensis (indicating the country or place of
growth or origin) indicating the area the plant was
originally found.

and is referable to M. petenensis rather than M. tondu-
zii.

S. acaulis has been reported by Spellman (1975)

been based on material of S. sceptrodes.

petals forming a hood over the column. Lateral
sepals free, enclosing the base of the lip. Lip longer
than the other segments and envelloping the column
at the base. Column erect.

lines.text: SUBTRIBE CRANICHIDINAE LINDL.
Terrestrial or epiphytic erect herbs. Roots clustered,
fleshy. Stems short. Leaves in a basal rosette, mem-
braneous, usually petiolate. Inflorescences terminal,
spicate, erect; peduncle with several sheaths.
Flowers few to many, in a raceme, rather small;
peduncle slender. Sepals and petals more or less
spreading, free; petals smaller than the sepals. Lip
uppermost in the flower, concave. Column short, with
a large rostellum; pollinia 2 but deeply divided; visci-
dium globose.
A genus of some 30 species, all native to the
American tropics and subtropics. One is known from
Belize.
ETymoLoGY. From the Greek kranos (helmet)
referring to the appearance of the concave lip.

sér. 3(3): 30 (1845). Type: Mexico, A. Richard & H.
Galeotti (holo. P).

SUBTRIBE HABENARIINAE BENTH.
Terrestrial herbs with one or more fleshy tuberoids
and fibrous roots. Stems erect, leafy or with leaves
only at, or near, the base. Leaves sheathing at the
base. Inflorescences terminal, 1- to many-flowered.
Flowers in a spike or raceme, usually green or white,
rarely showy. Dorsal sepal commonly erect and
hood-like. Lateral sepals spreading or reflexed.
Petals simple or bilobed. Lip simple or 3-lobed,
extended at the base into a spur; spur often long and
slender. Column very short; stigmas 2, stalked; rostel-
lum small, may be triangular, with divergent lateral
lobes; pollinia 2, clavate.
This is the largest genus of terrestrial orchids, with
about 600 species widely distributed in tropical and
subtropical parts of both the Old and New Worlds.
Thirteen are known from Belize, of which we have
seen eight.
Although generally inconspicuous, the flowers of
Habenaria are rather complex. In addition to the
petals and lip often being deeply divided, there are
two distinctly stalked stigmas at the base of the
column, and the viscidia (to which the pollinia are
attached) are often borne on long stalks derived from
the rostellum.
Most species of Habenaria are probably moth-
pollinated and, where the flowers have a fragrance,
this is generally most noticeable at night.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin habena (reins)
referring to the divisions of the petals and lip which,
in manyspecies, are strap-like.

12. Habenaris rodeiensis Barb. Rodr., Gen. Sp.
Orch. Nov. 2: 256 (1882). Type: Brazil, Rodeio,
J. Barbosa Rodrigues (holo. lost; painting from ori-
ginal plate t.799, photo. K!).
Plant terrestrial, rather slender, up to 48 cm tall, with
a tuberoid at the base. Stem leafy. Leaves several,
erect and clasping the stem, narrowly lanceolate,
glaucous, up to 9 cm long and 1.3 cm wide. Inflores-
cence commonly about 10- to 12-flowered, up to 11
cm long. Flowers fragrant, often more or less cleisto-
gamous; pedicellate ovaries up to 3.2 cm long. Sepals
pale green with darker green veins, concave, up to 1.2
cm long; dorsal sepal up to 4 mm wide; lateral sepal
up to 3 mm wide. Petals deeply bilobed, greenish-
white, up to 1 cm long; upper lobe connivent with the
dorsal sepal, up to 4.5 mm long and 2.5 mm wide;
lower lobe upcurved, slender, up to 2 mm long. Lip
deeply 3-lobed, pale green with a white base, up to
1.4 cm long; lateral lobes diverging, up to 3 mm long
and 0.8 mm wide; mid-lobe linear, up to 4 mm long
and 1.2 mm wide; spur slender, pale green with a
white base, up to 3.8 cm long. (Fig. 17G; Photo. 35).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, Venezuela and
Brazil.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Uncommon.
HABITAT. On well-drained slopes in open pine-
ridge between 700 and 1000m.
FLOWERING SEASON. Throughout the year, flow-
ering having been recorded in April, July, October
and December. Flowers open, or at least mature, from
the base of the raceme and individually last only a
few days.
ETymoLoGY. From Rodeio, in Brazil, where the
type specimen was found.
NoTEs. The short-lived and often more or less
cleistogamous flowers are a distinctive feature of the
Belize population. H. rodeiensis was not known from
anywhere in Central America prior to our collections
which were previouslyreported,incorrectly, as H.
leprieurii Rchb. f.

Plant terrestrial, up to 50 cm tall, with an ovoid
tuberoid at base. Stem leafy. Leaves few, more or less
erect, often clasping the stem, elliptic-lanceolate.
acuminate, up to 11 cm long and 1.4 cm wide;
sheaths on the lower part of the stem veined and
spotted with dark brown. Inflorescence 1-or 2-
flowered. Flowers greenish-cream with green sepals;
pedicellate ovaries erect, somewhat curved, ribbed,
up to 9 cm long. Sepals concave; dorsal sepal up to
1.2 cm long and 8 mm wide; lateral sepals reflexed,
acute, up to 1.4 cm long and 6 mm wide. Petals
bilobed almost to the base; upper lobe connivent with
the dorsal sepal, up to 1.2 cm long and 4 mm wide;
lower lobe spreading- upcurved, up to 1 cm long and
1.5 cm wide. Lip 3-lobed to the base, rather fleshy,
with the lobes all more or less linear and up to 1.4 cm
long and 3 mm wide; lateral lobes diverging; spur
pale green, slender at base, somewhat swollen to-
wards the apex, up to 6 cm long. (Fig. 17; Photo. 36).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Brazil and
Argentina.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo ( Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Districts.
Locally common.
HABITAT. On stony or sandy soils in open pine-
ridge between 50 and 1000m.
FLOWERING SEASON. June to September, and
January.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin trifida (divided into
three) in reference to the lip shape.

lines.text: TRIBE TRIPHOREAE DRESSLER
18. Psilochilus Barb. Rodr.
Terrestrial or epiphytic, plants with creeping rhi-
zomes. Roots adventitious, fleshy. Leaves membrana-
ceous with lax petioles. Inflorescences terminal, a
short spicate raceme. Flowers few. Sepals free,
keeled along the mid-vein. Petals free, not keeled
along mid-vein. Lip free, 3-lobed; disc with 3 longi-
tudinal calli. Column elongate, clavate; anther ter-
minal, 2-celled, mobile; pollinia 4.
This is a monotypic genus of tropical America.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek psilo (smooth) and
chilus (lipped) in reference to the appearance of the
lip.
Psilochilus macrophyllus (Lindl.) Ames, Orch.
Fasc. 7: 45 (1922). Type: locality unknown, Linden
(holo. K-LINDL.!).
Pogonia macrophylla Lindl. in Ann. Mag. Nat. Hist.
P. physurifolia Rchb. f. in Nederl. Kruidk. Arch. 4:
Plant terrestrial or epiphytic, with fleshy roots. Stem
branched, ascending. Leaves rigid, membranaceous,
oval-elliptic, up to 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Inflores-
cence terminal, racemose, 1- to 2-flowered; bracts
leafy, up to 2 cm long and 1.5 cm wide. Flowers
ringent with greenish sepals, greenish- white petals
and white lip. Sepals stiff and fleshy; dorsal sepal up
to 1.9 cm long and 3 mm wide; lateral sepals up to 1.8
cm long and 3 mm wide. Petals thinner than the
sepals, up to 1.8 cm long and 3 mm wide. Lip
3-lobed, up to 1.6 cm long and 8 mm wide; lateral
lobes acute; mid-lobe with serrate margins. Column
with 2 conspicuous broad apical teeth on the side of
the rostellum. (Fig. 18).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Central
America to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo, Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On leaf litter over sandy soil on the
forest floor and on mossy tree branches about 3 m
above the ground.
FLOWERING SEASON. December.
ETymoLoGY. From the Greek macrophyllus
(large-leaved).
NoTE. Reported by Catling & Catling (1988).

SUBTRIBE VANILLINAE LINDL.
19. Epistephium Kunth
Terrestrial herbs. Stems tall, simple or branched. Lea-
ves chartaceous to coriaceous, usually sessile or
cordate-clasping, strongly veined. Inflorescences ter-
minal or, rarely, axillary, racemose, many-flowered.
Flowers large; bracts short; apex of ovary with an
urceolate cup. Sepals subequal, free. Petals rather
similar to sepals but sometimes larger. Lip adnate to
the column, obovate, simple or slightly 3-lobed, en-
clasping the base of the column. Column long, dilated
above, broadly 3-lobed at apex. Capsule oblong-
cylindric.
A genus of about 20 species known from Belize,
Trinidad and northern South America. One is known
from Belize.
ETyMoLoGY. From the Greek epi (upon, above)
and stefos (a crown, wreath) in reference to the
crown-like growth that remains at the apex of the
ovary.

23. Eulophia R.Br. ex Lindl.
Terrestrial or rarely epiphytic herbs. Rhizome stout,
in the tropical Americas always with corm-like an-
nual segments. Leaves several, from the apex of the
corm, usually plicate, sheathing at the base.
Inflorescences from the base of the corm, erect,
single or, rarely, branching. Flowers small to large
and showy. Sepals spreading to reflexed. Petals often
more or less erect. Lip joined to the column foot,
3-lobed, commonly crested, pouch-like or spurred at
the base. Column basally extended into a foot; polli-
nia 2, often deeply cleft, waxy.
A large genus of over 200 species, widespread in
the tropics but most numerous in Africa. One is
known from Belize.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek eu (well) and lo-
phos (plume) referring to the crested lip.
Eulophia alta (L) Fawc. & Rendle, Fl. Jamaica 1:

Dendrobium longifolium Kunth, Nov. Gen. & Sp. 1:
Eulophia longifolia (Kunth) Schltr. in Orchideen:
Plant terrestrial, large, erect, up to 1.5 m tall. Corms
up to 6 cm in diameter. Leaves linear-elliptic, promi-
nently veined, acuminate, up to 1.2m long and 8 cm
wide. Inflorescence from the base of the corm, loose-
ly many-flowered; peduncle stout, up to 1 m long and
1.2 cm in diameter, provided with several large
sheaths. Flowers in a raceme; pedicellate ovaries
slender, up to 2.5 cm long. Sepals brownish-green,
keeled, up to 7 mm wide above the middle; dorsal
sepal up to 2.1 cm long; lateral sepals joined to the
sides of the column-foot and directed upwards, up to
2.4 cm long. Petals curved over the column, greenish
suffused with maroon, up to 1.7 cm long and 8 mm
wide. Lip pouch-like at the base, up to 1.9 cm long
and 1.7 cm across the lateral lobes when spread, with
two erect flap-like projections below the middle;
lateral lobes erect, greenish suffused with maroon,
rounded at the apex; mid-lobe decurved, maroon,
with undulate margins and several rows of papillae
along the veins. Column curved, green, with a broad
maroon foot, up to 9 mm long. (Fig. 23; Photo. 43).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Throughout the Ameri-
can tropics and subtropics, as well as Central and
West Africa.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Orange Walk, Cayo,
Stann Creek and Toledo Districts. Locally common.
HABITAT. In more or less open areas up to 200 m.
It favours heavy, moisture-retentive soils and often
found along roadsides or on cleared land reverting to
bush.
FLOWERING SEASON. September to February.
Flowers last up to a month.
EtymoLoGY. From the Latin altus (tall) in refer-
ence to the size of the plant.
NOTES. Although large, non-flowering plants are
easily overlooked as they greatly resemble the seed-
lings of various palms. The leaves die down during,
or soon after, the flowering period and the new shoot
is produced about May (the end of the dry season).
The separate inflorescence does not appear until Sep-
tember or October but then develops rapidly.

29 Cycnoches
Plants frequently produce both male and female
flowers but usually in separate racemes and at differ-
ent times. Mixed racemes and hermaphrodite flowers
occasionally occur. In both this genus and Catase-
tum, light intensity has been shown to influence sex
expression (Gregg, 1975). Plants in full sunlight are
more likely to produce female inflorescences than
those growing in shade.
The pollination mechanism involves a bee, from
the genus Euglossa, landing on the lip of a male
flower. The lip, which has a flexible claw, swings
down under the weight of the bee, causing the bee's
abdomen to touch the anther-cap, which discharges
the pollinia. When the bee then visits a female flower
it lands on the lip, attracted by the odour located at the
apex of the column, and when dropping off, the
pollinia are caught by the finger-like rostellar pro-
cesses of the column (van de Pijl & Dodson, 1966).
ETYmoLoGY. From the Greek kyknos (swan) and
auchen (neck) referring to the slender, curved column
of the male flower.

raceme, medium sized to large, unisexual and dimor-
phic. Sepals and petals similar. Lip uppermost in the
flower, simple or variously lobed. Column stout or
slender, curved, more or less club- shaped; pollinia 2,
waxy, ovoid, sulcate.
A genus of about 12 species, all in the American
tropics. Two are known from Belize. They are com-
monly known as 'swan orchids'.

29 Cycnoches
Plants frequently produce both male and female
flowers but usually in separate racemes and at differ-
ent times. Mixed racemes and hermaphrodite flowers
occasionally occur. In both this genus and Catase-
tum, light intensity has been shown to influence sex
expression (Gregg, 1975). Plants in full sunlight are
more likely to produce female inflorescences than
those growing in shade.
The pollination mechanism involves a bee, from
the genus Euglossa, landing on the lip of a male
flower. The lip, which has a flexible claw, swings
down under the weight of the bee, causing the bee's
abdomen to touch the anther-cap, which discharges
the pollinia. When the bee then visits a female flower
it lands on the lip, attracted by the odour located at the
apex of the column, and when dropping off, the
pollinia are caught by the finger-like rostellar pro-
cesses of the column (van de Pijl & Dodson, 1966).
ETYmoLoGY. From the Greek kyknos (swan) and
auchen (neck) referring to the slender, curved column
of the male flower.

2. Cycnoches ventricosum Batem., Orch. Mex.
Guat.: t. 5 (1837). Type: Guatemala, Ure Skinner s.n.
(holo. K!).
Plant epiphytic, stout, erect or spreading, up to 60 cm
tall. Pseudobulbs up to 30 cm long and 4 cm in
diameter though commonly less. Leaves elliptic to
narrowly oblanceolate, acuminate, up to 45 cm long
and 10 cm wide. Male inflorescence arching, several-
flowered, up to 40 cm long. Flowers fragrant. Sepals
and petals yellowish-green; dorsal sepal spreading,
up to 7 cm long and 1.6 cm wide; lateral sepals and
petals reflexed, up to 6 cm long and 2.2 cm wide. Lip
lanceolate-elliptic above an elongate slender base,
markedly convex, creamy white, shading to pale
green at the apex, fleshy, with a dark green basal
patch around a small callus, up to 5 cm long and 1.8
cm wide. Column slender, up to 4 cm long. Female
inflorescence erect or spreading, commonly 1-or
2-flowered, up to 14 cm long. Flowers heavily fra-
grant, similar to the male flowers. Sepals up to 2.4 cm
wide. Petals up to 2.8 cm wide. Column stout, about 2
cm long. (Fig. 30; Photo. 51, 52).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo, Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees, stumps and rotten logs in
moist broad-leaved forest, pastures and orchards be-
tween 50 and 150 m.
PLOWERING SEASON. July to February. Male
flowers last about a week, female flowers up to three
weeks. Plants lose their leaves during the winter
months and will occasionally flower when leafless.
EtymoLogY. from the Latin ventricosus (bellied
out below, distended, expanded) in reference to the
lip shape.
NoTEs. Material illustrated by Halcrow & Hal-
crow (1967) under the name C. warscewiczii appears
to represent the first record of this species in Belize.
C. warscewiczii Rchb. f., which is very closely
30 Mormodes
related to C. ventricosum, is probably restricted to
Costa Rica and Panama and differs in the slender
basal portion of the lip (claw) being shorter and the
callus being more protruberant.
Another closely allied species, C. chlorochilon
Klotzsch, was included by Spellman et al. (1975) on
their checklist of Belize monocotyledons. In this
case, the known distribution is northern South Amer-
ica and the lip is oblong-elliptic with virtually no
claw, quite unlike anything we have seen. Allen
(1952) treated both C. warscewiczii and C. chlorochi-
lon as varieties of C. ventricosum.
Epiphytic or terrestrial herbs. Pseudobulbs oblong,
Heshy, several-leaved. Leaves distichous, elongate,
plicate. Inflorescences lateral, 1 to several, from the
nodes of the pseudobulbs, racemose. Flowers showy,
often polymorphic. Sepals and petals free, spreading
or reflexed. Lip entire, 3-lobed, hairless or slightly
hairy; side lobes reflexed; mid-lobe apiculate. Col-
umn thick, erect, twisted to one side in male flowers;
pollinia 4, waxy, oblong.
A genus of about 20 species in Central and South
America. Two are known from Belize.
The pollination mechanism of the genus Mor-
modes is interesting (van der Pijl & Dodson, 1966).
Male euglossine bees, attracted by the flower's
odour, land on the lip and disturb the apex of the
column, which is twisted. The anther-cap acts as a
hinge and swings the pollinaria up onto the bee's
back. The stipe, which is coiled at this stage, gradual-
ly uncurls, and, after about thirty minutes, is in the
correct position to be placed on the stigma.
ETyMoLoGY. From the Greek mormo (phantom)
and eides (looking like) referring to the grotesque
appearance of the flowers.

cm wide. Lip fleshy, folded and twisted, interior
chocolate-brown within and strongly veined, pink on

Plant epiphytic, small, creeping to hanging, often in
clumps. Stems freely to densely branched, leafy
throughout and concealed by the imbricating leaf-
sheaths, up to 12 cm long and 1.5 mm in diameter.
Leaves distichous, persistent, prominently hairy
along the margins, dark green with a prominent mid-
vein beneath, 2-2.5 mm apart, up to 9 mm long
(including the sheath), blade up to 6 mm long and 2
mm wide. Inflorescence 1-flowered, from the axils of
the upper leaves; peduncle very slender, up to 6 mm
long. Flower not obviously scented, small, scarcely
opening, greenish-yellow; ovary covered in white
fleshy hairs and partly hidden by a small bract. Sepals
and petals similar, pale green, up to 5.5 mm long and
2.5 mm wide. Lip whitish with a slight purple suffu-
sion, incurved, more or less anchor-shaped when
flattened, with a narrow base and two slender
backward-directed lateral lobes. Column long for the
flower, up to 4 mm long. (Fig. 33K; Photo. 56).

Belize to Honduras, and Costa Rica.

clumps. Stems freely to densely branched, leafy
throughout and concealed by the imbricating leaf-
sheaths, up to 12 cm long and 1.5 mm in diameter.
Leaves distichous, persistent, prominently hairy
along the margins, dark green with a prominent mid-
vein beneath, 2-2.5 mm apart, up to 9 mm long
(including the sheath), blade up to 6 mm long and 2
mm wide. Inflorescence 1-flowered, from the axils of
the upper leaves; peduncle very slender, up to 6 mm
long. Flower not obviously scented, small, scarcely
opening, greenish-yellow; ovary covered in white
fleshy hairs and partly hidden by a small bract. Sepals
and petals similar, pale green, up to 5.5 mm long and
2.5 mm wide. Lip whitish with a slight purple suffu-
sion, incurved, more or less anchor-shaped when
flattened, with a narrow base and two slender
backward-directed lateral lobes. Column long for the
flower, up to 4 mm long. (Fig. 33K; Photo. 56).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Cuba, the West Indies,
Belize to Honduras, and Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in wet evergreen forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. September and October.
EtymologY. From the Greek hystrix (a por-
cupine).

Stem simple or branched, compressed, concealed by
leaf-sheaths, up to 60 cm long; aerial roots may be
produced from the leaf bases anywhere along the
stem. Leaves distichous, persistent, about 7 mm
apart, with imbricating leaf-sheaths, olive green, up
to 2 cm long and 7 mm wide. Inflorescence 1-

wards the end of the stem. Flowers on slender
peduncle of up to 1 cm long, slightly fragrant, up to

Sepals and petals similar; sepals orange, up to 1.4 cm
long and 4.5 mm wide; petals pale orange spotted
with reddish-purple, up to 1.2 cm long and 4 mm

Stem branched, compressed, concealed by leaf-
sheaths, up to 20 cm long and 2.5 mm in diameter;
aerial roots produced freely along the stem. Leaves
dictichous, persistent, elliptic, spreading, usually
about 4-5 mm apart; leaf-sheaths clasping the stem,
spotted with dark green; leaf blades up to 1.3 cm long
and 5 mm wide, mid-vein prominent beneath. In-
florescence 1-flowered, produced from the base of
the leaf axil towards the end of the stem; peduncle
slender, up to 8 mm long. Flowers not fragrant; ovary
muricate, partly obscured by a small floral bract,
about 1 mm long. Sepals and petals similar, incurved,
pale green spotted with dark purple sepals up to 1.1
cm long and 4 mm wide; petals narrower, up to 2.5
mm wide. Lip white, densely spotted with purple,
narrow base, anchor-shaped with two slender lateral
lobes slightly above the middle, incurved. Column

6. Maxillaria confusa Ames & Schweinf. in Ames,
Sched. Orch. 8: 57 (1925). Type: Costa Rica, Peralta,
C. H. Lankester 908 (holo. AMES 28689).
Plant epiphytic, small, up to 13 cm tall. Roots numer-
ous, fibrous, branched. Pseudobulbs up to 1.6 cm
long, monophyllous, concealed by a pair of imbricat-
ing distichous leaf-bearing sheaths. Leaves elliptic-
oblong, petioled, up to 10 cm long and 2.2 cm wide;
petiole laterally flattened, up to 2.2 cm long. Inflores-
cence shorter than the leaves, 1-flowered; peduncle
filiform, up to 4.5 cm long. Flowers large, erect,
white, lateral lobes of lip with red-violet nerves on
the upper half. Lateral sepals triangular-lanceolate,
up to 2 cm long and 7.2 mm wide, many-nerved,
forming a mentum with the column-foot; dorsal sepal
up to 2 cm long and 4.9 mm wide. Petals lanceolate,
up to 1.8 cm long and 3.7 mm wide. Lip small, erect,
3-lobed at apex, up to 1.2 cm long and 6 mm wide,
sides upcurving; callus lingulate. Column extended
into a long foot, short, stout, up to 4 mm long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, Nicaragua,
Costa Rica and Panama.

common.

Plant usually epiphytic, variable, in clumps, pseudo-
bulbs produced in close succession from the creeping
rhizome. Pseudobulbs grooved, somewhat flattened,
subtended by papery sheaths, up to 5.5 cm long and
2.5 cm wide, unifoliate. Leaves strap-like, leathery,
up to 40 cm long and 3.5 cm wide. Inflorescence 1 to
3, arising from the axils of the bracts surrounding the
pseudobulbs, each inflorescence is 1-flowered, up to
12 cm long; peduncle partially enclosed by tubular
bracts which are greenish, tinged with purple.
Flowers fleshy, up to 2.5 cm long and 2.8 cm in
diameter. Sepals somewhat fleshy, golden yellow to
black, deep maroon spotting within, flushed with
brownish red on the back, up to 3.8 cm long and 1.1
cm in diameter; lateral sepals forming a short men-
tum with the column-foot. Petals narrowly lanceo-
late, pale yellow with a reddish-brown tip, curved
inwards with tips touching, forming a hood, up to 2.3
cm long and 0.4 cm wide. Lip 3-lobed about the
middle, up to 3 cm long and 1 cm wide; side lobes
short, bluntly triangular and clasping the column;
callus between side lobes, sulcate. Column stout, up
to 1.5 cm long. (Fig. 46M; Photo 68).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras,
and Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (includ-
ing the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve). Rare.

Plant epiphytic with approximate, compressed,
rugose, monophyllous pseudobulbs. Pseudobulbs up
to 4.5 cm tall and 3.5 cm wide. Leaves leathery, up to
35 cm long and 3.5 cm wide; petiole conduplicate, up
to 3 cm long. Inflorescence 1-flowered from the base

creamy white sepals and petals, an orange lip with a
red-orange callus. Sepals elliptic, apiculate; dorsal
sepal up to 1.8 cm long and 0.9 cm wide; lateral
sepals up to 1.7 cm long and 0.8 cm wide. Petals
elliptic, up to 1.6 cm long and 0.6 cm wide. Lip

clavate, up to 8 mm long. (Fig. 44, 41L).

Nicaragua.

specimen.

Plant epiphytic, straggly, more or less hanging. Rhi-

to 2.8 cm long. Lip small, continuous with the
column-foot, cuneate-obovate, up to 8 mm long;
lateral lobes rounded, upcurved, whitish marked with
orange; mid-lobe almost semicircular, yellow; callus
linear, white, covered with orange papillae at base.

fair) in reference to the flowers.

Maxillaria augustifolia Hook., Ic. Pl. 4: t. 348
Plant epiphytic, a cluster of prostrate scaly rhizomes.
Pseudobulbs ovoid, 3 cm apart on the rhizome, dark
green, up to 4 cm long and 1.5 cm wide, unifoliate,
subtended by several sheaths. Leaves linear, grass-
green, up to 20 cm long and 1 cm wide. Inflorescence
1-flowered, subtended by several sheaths, from the
bases of the pseudobulbs. Flowers not fragrant, very
variable in both size and colour; pedicellate ovary up
to 3 cm long. Sepals and petals lemon- to golden-
yellow; petals often tinged with reddish-brown on the
outside, curl back at the tips, up to 1.4 cm long and
0.4 cm wide; sepals up to 1.7 cm long and 0.6 cm
wide; lateral sepals forming a mentum with the
column-foot. Lip deep reddish-brown tipped with
yellow, fleshy, erect, fleshy, obscurely 3-lobed in the
middle, rounded to truncate at apex, up to 1.3 cm long
and 0.6 cm wide; disc with a triangular-subquadrate
glossy callus. Column semiterete, arcuate, up to 1 cm
long. (Fig. 47; Photo. 81).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo (including
the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Common.
HABITAT. On trees in moist forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. July to March. Flowers last
about a week.
40 Mormolyca
ETyMoLoGY. From the Latin variabilis (variable)
in reference to the variable size and colour of the
flowers.
NoTE. M. variabilis is known, in some parts of
Guatemala, as "La Gloria'.
Epiphytic herbs. Rhizome rather short. Pseudobulbs
1- to 4-leaved. Leaves leathery. Inflorescences from
the base of the pseudobulb or the axils of bracts on the
rhizome, 1-flowered; peduncles elongate, slender.
Sepals free. Petals and lip smaller than the sepals. Lip
hinged to the base of the column, simple or 3-lobed,
with a median callus. Column without a foot; pollinia
4, waxy; viscidium lunate.
A genus of six species distributed from Mexico to
Brazil and Peru. One is known from Belize.
The genus is closely allied to Maxillaria but sepa-
rated on the basis of the flowers lacking a column-
foot and mentum.
ETymoLoGY. From the Greek mormolyca (hob-
goblin) alluding to the supposedly grotesque appear-
ance and colouration of the flower.

and 3 cm wide, unifoliate, subtended by prominent
sheaths when young; sheaths brown, papery. Leaves
linear-elliptic, up to 35 cm long and 3.5 cm wide.
Inflorescence few, more or less erect, produced in
succession; peduncle wiry, persistent, up to 28 cm
long, provided with several papery sheaths. Flowers
greenish-yellow, purple-veined; pedicellate ovaries
slender, up to 4.5 cm long. Sepals up to 1.8 cm long;

wide; lateral sepals directed downwards, curved to-

directed upwards beneath the dorsal sepal, curved
towards each other and overlapping at the tips, with
strongly recurved margins, up to 1.4 cm long and 5
mm wide. Lip 3-lobed below the middle, up to 9 mm
long and 5 mm wide; lateral lobes small, triangular;
mid-lobe strongly decurved, suffused with maroon,

most confusing and has been reviewed by Whitten

tion is rather vague. This has meant that many reports
of G. quinquenervis have been inaccurate.

2. Stanhopea graveolens Lindl. in Bot. Reg. 26:
Misc.59 (1840). Type: of uncertain provenance, cult.

Plant epiphytic or rarely lithophytic, medium-sized
Pseudobulbs ovoid-conical to rhomboidal, sulcate,
somewhat compressed, up to 7 cm long and 4 cm in
diameter, 1-leaved at apex. Leaves plicate, broadly
elliptic-lanceolate to obovate-elliptic, acute, up to 50
cm long and 17.5 cm wide. Inflorescence pendulous,
up to 9-flowered; peduncle terete, from base of pseu-
dobulb; sheaths inflated, up to 6 cm long. Flowers
large, showy, fragrant, hanging, cream or greenish-
white, spotted with purple on sepals and petals; epi-
chile of lip with a large maroon spot on each side of
hypochile. Dorsal sepal reflexed, ovate-elliptic,
rounded at apex, up to 6.3 cm long and 3.5 cm wide;
lateral sepals reflexed, oblique, concave, up to 6.5 cm
long and 4.5 cm wide, joined in the basal 1 cm. Petals
recurved, narrowly oblong, acute, up to 5.5 cm long
and 2.3 cm wide, with undulate margins. Lip very
fleshy, tripartite, up to 5 cm long; hypochile rectangu-
lar, saccate; mesochile of two fleshy porrect horns;
epichile ovate-cordate, acute. Column arcuate,
winged, up to 5 cm long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras and
El Salvador.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo (Mountain Pine
Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees in riverine forest.

FLOWERING SEASON. November.
ETYMoLoGY. From the Latin graveolens (strong
smelling) in reference to the powerful and rather
offensive scent of the flowers.
NoTes. For many years S. graveolens was consi-
dered to be a synonym of the common S. oculata but
Dodson (1975a) has clarified the distinction between
the two. He has also clarified the distinction between
the often confused S. graveolens and S. wardii, the
latter having smaller flowers with a shorter lip and is
not found further north than Nicaragua.
3. Stanhopea inodora Lodd. ex Lindl. in Bot. Reg.
31: t.65 (1845). Type: Mexico, Loddiges (holo. based

Plant epiphytic. Pseudobulbs heavily ribbed, mono-
phyllous, up to 5 cm long and 3.5 cm wide. Leaves
elliptic-lanceolate, up to 30 cm long and 11 cm wide;
pedicel up to 4 cm long. Inflorescence pendent,
several-flowered. Flowers showy with creamy white
sepals and petals, lightly spotted red, the basal half of
the hypochile orange with more or less distinct eyes;
lip white with very faint spots on the epichile and at
the base of the horn, not fragrant. Dorsal sepal lan-
ceolate, apiculate, up to 8 cm long and 4.5 cm wide;
lateral sepals broadly lanceolate, apiculate, up to 7.5
cm long and 4.5 cm wide. Petals linear-lanceolate
with undulate margins, up to 7 cm long and 2 cm
wide. Lip with a circular opening to the almost naked
cavity, up to 3 cm long and 2 cm wide; epichile up to 3
cm long and wide. Column winged, up to 6 cm long
and 2 cm wide; column-wings more than half as wide
as the column.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico, Belize and
Nicaragua.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in damp montane forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. May to September.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin in (not) and odorus
(scented, smelling).

GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Columbia
and Brazil.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo and Toledo Dis-

HABITAT. On trees, stumps, rotten logs, on rocks
or in moist to wet broad-leaved forest between 400
and 750m.
FLOWERING SEASON. June to October. Flowers
last about four days.
EtymoLoGY. From the Latin oculatus (eyed, with
an eye) in reference to the two large maroon 'eyes' on
the base of the lip.

SUBTRIBE ORNITHOCEPHALINAE SCHLTR.
Epiphytic plants without pseudobulbs. Stems short,
completely covered with distichous, imbricating
leaf-sheaths. Leaves fleshy, equitant, arranged in a
fan-shape. Inflorescences axillary, racemose, few- to
several-flowered. Flowers small. Sepals and petals
similar, free. Lip entire or lobed; callus basally thick-
ened, inflexed in front. Column short, without wings
or a foot; anther beaked; pollinia 4, waxy.
A genus of about 50 species distributed throughout
the American tropics. Two are known from Belize.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek ornithos (bird) and
kephale (head) alluding to the curious shape of the
column-apex, which resembles a bird's head.

Plant epiphytic, small and fan-shaped, without pseu-
dobulbs, normally pendent. Leaves somewhat fleshy,
equitant, up to eighteen in number, linear, acute, up to
10 cm long and 6 mm wide; sheaths imbricated, up to
1.5 cm long. Inflorescence 1 or more per plant, ra-
cemose, many-flowered, from the axil of the leaf-
sheath, up to 11 cm long. Flowers not fragrant, small,
white with a greenish lip; pedicellate ovaries
glabrous, up to 5 mm long. Sepals spreading, subor-
bicular, dorsally carinate, glabrous, up to 2.3 mm
long and 1.8 mm wide. Petals cuneate-flabellate, up
to 3.5 mm long and 4.2 mm wide. Lip deeply 3-
lobed, base triangular-cordate, up to 5 mm in diame-
ter. Column short, fleshy, up to 3 mm long; rostellum
produced into a long beak. Capsule broadly 6-
winged. (Fig. 55; Photo. 94).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Costa Rica,
and Trinidad.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Orange Walk, Cayo (in-
cluding the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve), Stann
Creek and Toledo Districts. Fairly common.

down on trunks in well shaded situations.
FLOWERING SEASON. March to May.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin gladiatus (sword-

47 Brassia
SUBTRIBE ONCIDIINAE BENTH.
Epiphytic, occasionally lithophytic or terrestrial
herbs. Rhizome stout, creeping. Pseudobulbs ovoid to
cylindrical, 1- to 3-leaved. Leaves linear or elliptic-
oblong, leathery. Inflorescences from the base of a
pseudobulb, few- to many-flowered. Flowers in a
raceme, often showy. Sepals spreading, free, long and
narrow. Petals similar to the sepals but shorter. Lip
simple, with a basal callus. Column short, stout,
wingless; pollinia 2, obovoid.
A genus of about 20 species, widely distributed in
the American tropics. Two are known from Belize.
This genus is frequently cultivated and often
known as 'spider orchids' on account of their long
slender sepals. The resemblance of the flowers to
spiders is probably not accidental since spider-
hunting wasps have been observed to attack them
and, in the process, effect pollination. Dodson (1990)
has observed female wasps of the genera Pepsis and
Campsomeris pollinating species of Brassia. These
wasps hunt spiders and paralyse them by stinging,
then carry them to their nests and lay their eggs on
them. The larva of the wasps consume the fresh, but
paralysed, tissues of the spider. Pollination is effected
by an attempt to 'capture' the column and in the
unsuccessful attempt to drag away their 'prey' the
pollinia are placed on the head of the wasp.
Brassia is allied to Oncidium with which some
species have been crossed to give rise to the hybrid
genus x Brassidium.
ETyMoLoGY. Named after William Brass (died
1783), the English plant collector, botanical artist and
gardener to the 1st Duke of Northumberland.

lines.text: 50. Leochilus Knowles & Westcott
Plants small, tufted, epiphytic herbs with pseudobul-
bous stems. Pseudobulbs covered by 1 to several
leaf-sheaths at base and 1- to 2-leaved above. Leaves
leathery, lanceolate. Inflorescences racemose or pani-
culate, laxly few- flowered. Flowers small, inconspi-
cuous. Sepals and petals spreading, free or connate.
Lip adnate to base of column, entire or 3-lobed; callus
fleshy. Column lacking a foot, bearing stelidia on
each side near middle, truncate at apex; rostellum
elongate; pollinia 2, waxy.
A genus of about 15 species distributed from the
West Indies and Mexico to Argentina. One is known
from Belize.
Leochilus is allied to Oncidium but differs in that
the anther is produced in front into a membranceous
appendage equalling or mostly longer than the locule
(Bechtel et al., 1992).
ETyMoLogY. From the Greek leios (smooth) and
cheilos (lip) referring to the smooth surface of the
lip.
Leochilus labiatus (Sw.) Kuntze in Rev. Gen. Pl.: 656
(1891). Type: Jamaica, Swartz (holo. UPS).
Epidendrum labiatum Sw., Prodr: 124 (1788).
Rodriguezia cochlearis Lindl. in Ann. Nat. Hist. 5:
Leochilus gracilis Schltr. in Fedde, Repert. Sp. Nov.
Plant epiphytic, small, erect, up to 25 cm tall; the
entire plant often tinged with red. Pseudobulbs
clustered, ovoid, unifoliate, up to 20 mm long and 12
mm wide, subtended by scarious leaf-sheaths. Leaves
from apex of pseudobulb, broadly elliptic, up to 7 cm
long and 2 cm wide. Inflorescence from base of
pseudobulb, racemose, few-flowered; peduncle with
lanceolate bracts of up to 9 mm long. Flowers small,
translucent, yellow or pale green, suffused with red-
brown; pedicellate ovary up to 10 mm long. Dorsal
sepal ovate-elliptic, arcuate over the column, up to
6.5 mm long and 3 mm wide; lateral sepals deflexed,
50 Leochilus
united to the middle, up to 6.5 mm long and 1.5 mm
wide above the point of union. Petals projected fore-
wards, elliptic-oblong, up to 6 mm long and 2.8 mm
wide. Lip strongly arcuate, spreading above, base
appressed against column, up to 8 mm long and 4.5
mm wide; disc fleshly-thickened. Column thick, up to
3 mm long, with a denticulate membrane at apex and
a slender linear arm on each side about the middle.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Belize
to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Stann Creek District.
Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees in moist valley regions or open
mountain forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. March to June.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin labiatus (lipped, lip-
shaped).
NoTE. Reported by Catling & Catling (1988).
Epiphytic herbs. Rhizome short, creeping. Pseudo-
bulbs slender, clustered, unifoliate. Leaves linear-
lanceolate, leathery or fleshy. Inflorescences from the
base of the pseudobulb, few- to many-flowered.
Flowers in a raceme. Sepals and petals similar, lan-
ceolate, spreading, free. Lip joined to the base of the
column, simple or 3-lobed, concave, with a basal
callus. Column erect, apex with an oblong hood over
the anther; pollinia 2, pyriform; stipe linear-oblong;
viscidium small.
A genus of about five species, all in the American
tropics. One is known from Belize.
Leucohyle has been included within Trichopilia by
some recent authors but is distinguished by its more
slender growth, the smaller flowers and the lateral
lobes of the lip, which do not form a tube enclosing
the column.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek leucos (white) and
hyle (wood or stuff) probably referring to the white
indumentum on the floral axis.

Small to large epiphytic, lithophytic or terrestrial
plants with short to long rhizomes. Pseudobulbs

sheaths. Leaves flat to terete, membranaceous to

pollinia 2, waxy, deeply sulcate.
55. Oncidium Sw.
55 Oncidium
A large genus of over 400 species native to the
American tropics and subtropics. Eight are known
from Belize.
Many species of Oncidium are pollinated by an-
throphorid bees of the genus Centris, many of which
gather oil from the flower instead of, or as well as,
pollen. These bees display strong territorial behav-
iour. Male bees set up territories and drive away other
flying insects which invade their territory. When the
flowers of an Oncidium, which resemble insects,
move, the bees attack them, striking the flowers with
their heads. The viscidium attaches to the front of the
bee, between the compound eyes, and the stipe
depresses holding the pollinia in front of the bee. This
pollination mechanism is called pseudoantagonism
(van de Pijl & Dodson, 1966).
EtymologY. From the Greek onkos (a pad or
mass) referring to the fleshy warty callus on the lip of
many species.

lines.text: fleshy, deeply channelled, up to 30 cm long and 1.1
cm wide, tapering to a sharp point, dark green with
purple spots. Inflorescence from base of pseudobulb,
more or less erect, racemose, up to 16-flowered.
Flowers not fragrant, clustered, small, on the upper
third of the inflorescence, up to 2.5 cm long and 2 cm
wide. Sepals and petals similar, curved forewards at
the tip, greenish-yellow blotched with red-brown,
margins yellow and undulate; sepals up to 1.4 cm
long and 0.8 cm wide, spathulate; petals up to 1.3 cm
long and 0.6 cm wide, oblong. Lip 3-lobed, with the
mid-lobe the largest, yellow spotted with red-brown,
up to 2 cm long and 2.5 cm wide; callus between the
side lobes, walnut-like with a prominent central
ridge, white spotted with red-brown. Column short,
stout, whitish with purple spots, two small wings at
the apex, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 110).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Mexi-
co to Paraguay.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Very rare.
HABITAT. On trees in wet riverine forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. February. Flowers last about
three weeks.
EtymoLogY. Derivation not known.
5. Oncidium ensatum Lindl. in Bot. Reg. 28: Misc.
17 (1842). Type: Guatemala, cult. Loddiges (holo. K,
not located).
Plant terrestrial, usually tall and graceful. Pseudo-
bulbs in a small clump, flattened, up to 10 cm long
and 4 cm wide, bifoliate, subtended by broad over-
lapping sheaths. Leaves erect, linear-ensiform, up to
90 cm long and 3.5 cm wide, yellow-green, keeled.
Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb, en-
closed in sheathing bracts, paniculate, up to 2.5 m tall
with numerous widely spaced branches. Flowers
slightly fragrant, numerous, small, up to 2.8 cm long
and 2.2 cm wide. Sepals and petals similar,
chocolate-brown, tipped and edged with greenish-
yellow and with occasional yellow spotting,
somewhat reflexed with an undulate margin, up to 1.6
cm long and 7 mm wide. Lip bright yellow, side lobes
with a brown base, broadly violin-shaped, 3-lobed,
up to 1.8 cm long and 1.3 cm wide, mid-lobe sepa-
rated from side lobes by a broad isthmus; callus at the
base of the lip, tuberculate, fleshy. Column short,
fleshy, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 111).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo (including
the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Fairly common.
55 Oncidium
HABITAT. In open grassy areas (savanna), moun-
tain and coastal pine ridge areas, often in dense grass
associated with small bushes.
FLOWERING SEASON. December to May. Flowers
last two to three weeks.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin ensatus (sword-
shaped) in reference to the sword-shaped leaves.
NoTE. This species is unique among Belizean
Oncidiums in its obligate terrestrial habitat.
6. Oncidium lindenii Brongn. in Lem., Hort. Univ.
3: 372 (1842). Type: Mexico, Campeche, Linden s.n.
(holo. BR).
O. lindenii Lodd. ex Lindl., Sert. Orch.: sub.t.48,
n.101 (1841) nom. illeg.
Plant epiphytic, tall. Pseudobulbs small, often
covered with scarious sheaths, unifoliate. Leaves
thickened, ridgid, leathery, dark green and in-
distinctly spotted and blotched with purple, up to 30
cm long and 7 cm wide. Inflorescence arising from
the base of the pseudobulb, up to 110 cm long,
paniculate with one or more small branches, each
with several flowers; peduncle slender and wiry.
Flowers not fragrant, up to 2 cm in diameter. Sepals
and petals similar, brown with a greenish-white patch
at the base or spotted with brown on pale green. Lip
with a golden yellow base, side lobes glossy, very
dark magenta appearing almost black. Column short,
winged, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 112)
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On isolated trees and in riverine forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. March to June. Flowers last
three to five weeks.
ETYMOLOGY. Named after Jean Linden (1817-
1898), a Luxemburg born botanical explorer, orchid
collector, nurseryman at Ghent and founder of the
Horticulture Internationale in Brussels, who found
the type specimen.
7. Oncidium sphacelatum Lindl., Sert. Orch.:
sub.t.48 (1841). Type: Mexico, Hartweg (holo. K-
LINDL.! but specimen lacking provenance).
Plant epiphytic, in large clumps, often extremely
large masses. Pseudobulbs flattened, somewhat
ridged, up to 20 cm long and 5 cm wide, bearing
either one, or more usually two, leaves. Leaves rigid,
erect, up to 70 cm long and 5 cm wide, light green.

cm wide, tapering to a sharp point, dark green with
purple spots. Inflorescence from base of pseudobulb,
more or less erect, racemose, up to 16-flowered.
Flowers not fragrant, clustered, small, on the upper
third of the inflorescence, up to 2.5 cm long and 2 cm
wide. Sepals and petals similar, curved forewards at
the tip, greenish-yellow blotched with red-brown,
margins yellow and undulate; sepals up to 1.4 cm
long and 0.8 cm wide, spathulate; petals up to 1.3 cm
long and 0.6 cm wide, oblong. Lip 3-lobed, with the
mid-lobe the largest, yellow spotted with red-brown,
up to 2 cm long and 2.5 cm wide; callus between the
side lobes, walnut-like with a prominent central
ridge, white spotted with red-brown. Column short,
stout, whitish with purple spots, two small wings at
the apex, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 110).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Mexi-
co to Paraguay.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Very rare.
HABITAT. On trees in wet riverine forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. February. Flowers last about
three weeks.
EtymoLogY. Derivation not known.
5. Oncidium ensatum Lindl. in Bot. Reg. 28: Misc.
17 (1842). Type: Guatemala, cult. Loddiges (holo. K,
not located).
Plant terrestrial, usually tall and graceful. Pseudo-
bulbs in a small clump, flattened, up to 10 cm long
and 4 cm wide, bifoliate, subtended by broad over-
lapping sheaths. Leaves erect, linear-ensiform, up to
90 cm long and 3.5 cm wide, yellow-green, keeled.
Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb, en-
closed in sheathing bracts, paniculate, up to 2.5 m tall
with numerous widely spaced branches. Flowers
slightly fragrant, numerous, small, up to 2.8 cm long
and 2.2 cm wide. Sepals and petals similar,
chocolate-brown, tipped and edged with greenish-
yellow and with occasional yellow spotting,
somewhat reflexed with an undulate margin, up to 1.6
cm long and 7 mm wide. Lip bright yellow, side lobes
with a brown base, broadly violin-shaped, 3-lobed,
up to 1.8 cm long and 1.3 cm wide, mid-lobe sepa-
rated from side lobes by a broad isthmus; callus at the
base of the lip, tuberculate, fleshy. Column short,
fleshy, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 111).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo (including
the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Fairly common.
55 Oncidium
HABITAT. In open grassy areas (savanna), moun-
tain and coastal pine ridge areas, often in dense grass
associated with small bushes.
FLOWERING SEASON. December to May. Flowers
last two to three weeks.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin ensatus (sword-
shaped) in reference to the sword-shaped leaves.
NoTE. This species is unique among Belizean
Oncidiums in its obligate terrestrial habitat.
6. Oncidium lindenii Brongn. in Lem., Hort. Univ.
3: 372 (1842). Type: Mexico, Campeche, Linden s.n.
(holo. BR).
O. lindenii Lodd. ex Lindl., Sert. Orch.: sub.t.48,
n.101 (1841) nom. illeg.
Plant epiphytic, tall. Pseudobulbs small, often
covered with scarious sheaths, unifoliate. Leaves
thickened, ridgid, leathery, dark green and in-
distinctly spotted and blotched with purple, up to 30
cm long and 7 cm wide. Inflorescence arising from
the base of the pseudobulb, up to 110 cm long,
paniculate with one or more small branches, each
with several flowers; peduncle slender and wiry.
Flowers not fragrant, up to 2 cm in diameter. Sepals
and petals similar, brown with a greenish-white patch
at the base or spotted with brown on pale green. Lip
with a golden yellow base, side lobes glossy, very
dark magenta appearing almost black. Column short,
winged, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 112)
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On isolated trees and in riverine forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. March to June. Flowers last
three to five weeks.
ETYMOLOGY. Named after Jean Linden (1817-
1898), a Luxemburg born botanical explorer, orchid
collector, nurseryman at Ghent and founder of the
Horticulture Internationale in Brussels, who found
the type specimen.
7. Oncidium sphacelatum Lindl., Sert. Orch.:
sub.t.48 (1841). Type: Mexico, Hartweg (holo. K-
LINDL.! but specimen lacking provenance).
Plant epiphytic, in large clumps, often extremely
large masses. Pseudobulbs flattened, somewhat
ridged, up to 20 cm long and 5 cm wide, bearing
either one, or more usually two, leaves. Leaves rigid,
erect, up to 70 cm long and 5 cm wide, light green.
Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb, pani-
culate, much branched and many-flowered, up to

yellow and strongly blotched with brown in the lower
two thirds, reflexed at the top, undulate margins, up to

Column with small wings, fleshy, up to 6 mm long.
(Fig. 66; Photo. 113).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to El Salvador.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. All districts. Common.
HABITAT. On trees in forest and thicket.
FLOWERING SEASON. December to May. Flowers
last two to three weeks.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin sphacelatus (with
brown or blackish speckling) in reference to the
colouring of the sepals and petals.
8. Oncidium stipitatum Lindl. in Benth., Bot. Voy.
Sulph.: 172 (1846). Type: Panama, G.W. Barclay 958
(holo. BM!).
Plant epiphytic, tufted, often pendent. Pseudobulbs
small, usually unifoliate, up to 2 cm long and 1 cm
wide. Leaf long-linear, arcuate, semiterete, a single
groove runs down the centre of the leaf ending in a
sharp point, up to 70 cm long and 1.5 cm wide.
Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb, pani-
culate, up to 100 cm long. Flowers showy, numerous,
up to 2 cm in diameter and 1.8 cm wide; lip bright
yellow, sepals and petals yellow streaked with red,
column yellow with red markings. Sepals spreading,
reflexed, lanceolate; dorsal sepal hooded; lateral
sepals up to 0.8 cm long and 0.4 cm wide. Petals
spreading, lanceolate, up to 1 cm long and 0.5 cm
wide, undulate margins. Lip deeply 3-lobed, up to 1.8
cm long and 1.5 cm wide; lateral lobes linear-
lanceolate, acuminate, wing-like; mid-lobe larger
than lateral lobes, semiorbicular, margins undulate;
callus red-brown. Column winged, up to 1 cm long
and 0.3 cm wide; wings up to 0.4 cm wide.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize and Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees in open mountain forest at
about 650 m.
FLOWERING SEASON. Not known.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin stipitatus (provided
with a stalk).
NOTES. O. stipitatum was reported by Siegerist
(1984) on the basis of a specimen from Belize at EAP.
We have not seen this specimen and have not been
56 Psygmorchis
able to find any other reports from Belize. There are
no herbarium specimens of this plant at Kew and the
description has been taken from a drawing in the Kew
herbarium (Jones & Scully 644.62, Feb. 28, 1963/
487). The plant is very similar to O. ascendens and
differs in a number of minor characteristics. We have
not included it in the key.
56. Psygmorchis Dodson & Dressler
Dwarf epiphytes lacking pseudobulbs. Stem very
short. Leaves distichous in a fan, equitant, succulent.
Inflorescences lateral, 1-flowered. Flowers large for
plant, with a large yellow lip. Dorsal sepal and petals
free; lateral sepals partially united. Lip large, 4-lobed,
at right angles to column; callus basal. Column
winged, short; pollinia 2, hard, laterally attached to to
a long narrow stipe; viscidium 1.
A genus of about five species distributed in Central
and South America. One is known from Belize.
The genus Psygmorchis is a segregate of Oncidium
established by C. Dodson & R. Dressler in 1972. The
plants lack pseudobulbs, have iridiform leaves and
condensed inflorescences producing one flower at a
time.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek psygma (fan) and
orchis (an orchid) in reference to the characteristic
growth habit of the plant.
Psygmorchis pusilla (L) Dodson & Dressler in Phy-
tologia 24: 288 (1972). Type: Surinam, C. Dahlberg
(holo. S).
Epidendrum pusillum L., Sp. Pl., Ed.2, 2: 1352
Oncidium pusillum (L.) Rchb. f. in Walp. Ann. Bot.
O. iridifolium Kunth, Nov. Gen. Sp. Pl. 1: 344
Plant epiphytic, small, fan-shaped, occuring singly or
in a cluster, pendent, without pseudobulbs. Leaves
flattened, from a short rhizome, fleshy, sword-
shaped, up to 7 cm long and 1.5 cm wide. Inflores-
cence from the axils of the leaves, 1-flowered, usual-
ly with several bracts at the apex of the peduncle.
Flowers large and showy in relation to the size of the
plant, not fragrant, yellow with reddish spots on the
large lip and petals, up to 2.5 cm long and 2 cm wide;
pedicellate ovary up to 7 mm long. Sepals and petals
similar. Lip much larger than the sepals and petals,
3-lobed at the base; callus fleshy. Column short, thick,
up to 4 mm long. (Fig. 67; Photo. 114).

lines.text: GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Mexi-
co to northern South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo, Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees and notably in citrus planta-
tions.
FLOWERING SEASON. Intermittent throughout the
year. Flowers last several weeks.
EtymoLoGY. From the Latin pusillus (very small,
insignificant) in reference to the very small plant
S1Ze.
NOTES. This species has proved difficult to grow
in cultivation. The seed pods are large, up to 2.5 cm
long and 1.8 cm wide, and prominently 6-winged.
Epiphytic herbs. Rhizome short. Pseudobulbs
clustered, unifoliate. Leaves leathery. Inflorescences
from the base of the pseudobulb, 1- to few-flowered.
Flowers large and showy. Sepals and petals similar,
spreading, narrow, twisted or contorted. Lip joined to
the base of the column, more or less 3-lobed, with or
without a callus; lateral lobes forming a tube enclos-
ing the column. Column slender, clavate, erect, 2-
winged; pollinia 2, waxy; stipe broadly triangular.
A genus of about 25 species, all native to the
tropics of Central and South America. One is known
from Belize.
ETYMOLoGY. From the Greek trichos (hair) and
pilos (felt, felt-cap) referring to the fact that the anther
is concealed below a cap surmounted with three tufts
of hair.
Trichopilia tortilis Lindl., Introd. Nat. Syst. Bot.
ed.2: 446 (1836). Type: Mexico, G. Barker (holo.
K-LINDL.! but specimen lacking provenance).
Plant epiphytic, erect-spreading, up to 28 cm tall.
Pseudobulbs more or less oblong, strongly flattened,
up to 9 cm long and 2 cm wide, more or less enclosed
in sheaths when young; sheaths papery, brown-
spotted. Leaves narrowly elliptic, dark green, acute,
57. Trichopilia Lindl.
57 Trichopilia
folded at the base, up to 24 cm long and 4.6 cm wide.
Inflorescence 1- to 2-flowered; peduncle up to 8 cm
long, enclosed at base in several sheaths. Flowers
faintly fragrant; pedicellate ovaries up to 6 cm long.
Sepals and petals brownish-purple bordered with
pale green, twisted, up to 6 cm long and 1 cm wide.
Lip broadly obovate in outline, white spotted with
pink, yellow within the tubular portion, up to 5 cm
long and 4 cm wide across the lateral lobes when
spread; mid-lobe spreading, somewhat decurved,
notched at the apex, with undulate margins. Column
green at base, white above, up to 2 cm long. (Fig. 68;
Photo. 115).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Nicaragua.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in wet broad-leaved forest at
about 750 m.
FLOWERING SEASON. October to January. Flowers
last about two weeks.
ETyMoLoGY. From the Latin tortilis (twisted) in
reference to the twisted appearance of the sepals and
petals.
NotEs. The large and colourful flowers with their
strangely twisted sepals and petals are most attrac-
tive.
SUBTRIBE BLETIINAE BENTH.
Terrestrial or, rarely, epiphytic herbs. Pseudobulbs
corm-like. Leaves few, from the apex of the corm,
plicate, petiolate. Inflorescences from the side of the
corm. Flowers often showy. Sepals and petals simi-
lar, free, spreading. Lip joined to the column-foot,
simple or three-lobed, variously crested. Column
curved, more or less winged above, basally extended
into a short foot; pollinia 8, in 2 sets of 4, hard,
compressed.
A genus of about 30 closely allied species, all in
the American tropics and subtropics and with the
largest number in Mexico. One is known from Bel-
ize.

lines.text: Correll (1965) reported B. tenuifolia Ames & C.
Schweinf. as occuring in Belize from a collection by
Gentle (9736) on Colonel English Pine Ridge, Cayo
District. Catling & Catling (1988) have examined the
specimen in the Lundell Herbarium and found it to be
Encyclia bractescens.
EtymoLogY. Named after Don Luis Blet, an 18th
century Spanish pharmacist and botanist.
Bletia purpurea (Lam.) DC. in Mem. Soc. Phys.

64 Brassavola
SUBTRIBE LAELIINAE BENTH.
Epiphytic herbs, sometimes growing on rocks. Rhi-
zome commonly short. Stems slender or thickened
and pseudobulbous, unifolate, enclosed in sheaths
when young. Leaves fleshy. Inflorescences com-
monly terminal, rarely lateral, 1- to several-flowered.
Flowers large and showy. Sepals and petals similar.
Lip simple or three-lobed, tubular at base, more or
less enclosing the column, with or without a basal
callus. Column erect, short, mostly 2-winged; anther
operculate; pollinia 8.
A genus of about 15 species, all native to the
American tropics. Four are known from Belize.
The predominantly white or pale greenish flowers
are usually pollinated by moths.
Several species are widely cultivated and some
have been extensively used in the production of horti-
cultural hybrids. The majority of crosses have in-
volved species of Cattleya and Laelia, giving rise to
the hybrid genera x Brassocattleya, x Brassolaelia
and x Brassolaeliocattleya.
H.G. Jones (1975) revised the sectional limits of
Brassavola. Section Grandiflora, in which the leaves
are flat and broad, corresponds to Rhyncolaelia
Schltr. and was excluded by Schlechter (1919) from
his revision and by us here.
EtymoLogY. Named after the Venetian nobleman
and botanist Antonio Musa Brassavola (1500-1555).

GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, Guatemala(?)
and Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize and Cayo (in-
cluding the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) Districts.
Locally common.
HABITAT. On granite outcrops, cliffs, ravine sides
and limestone rocks between 100 and 1000 m.
Rarely found on trees in pine/oak forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. July to October. Flowers last
about two weeks.
EtymoLogY. Named after J.C. Bowring (1821-
1893) of Windsor, England, who was an enthusiastic
amateur grower of orchids.
NoTES. Almost confined to the Mountain Pine
Ridge Reserve where it is often found in association
with Encyclia belizensis subsp. belizensis. Halcrow
& Halcrow (1967) reported a white-flowered form
but we have never seen it. C. bowringiana has been
considered by some authors to be no more than a
geographic variant of the more widespread C. skin-
neri Batem. It differs from C. skinneri principally in
having bulbous stem bases and in tending to grow
larger in favourable situations such as along the Rio
On, the type locality. The flowering season is also
atypical of C. skinneri which is normally spring-
fowering.
Several authors have reported both C. bowringiana
and C. skinneri from Belize but we have been quite
unable to find the latter in the field. Plants on exposed
rocks are generally much smaller than those in shel-
tered ravines and a rare individual may flower outside
the normal season but every one of the many we have
examined has proved to have the bulbous stem bases
typical of C. bowringiana.
Epiphytic herbs. Pseudobulbs clustered, elongate,
several-jointed, bearing 2- several terminal leaves,
more or less enclosed in sheaths when young. Leaves
leathery. Inflorescences terminal, few- to many-
flowered; peduncle elongate. Flowers in a raceme
and rather showy. Sepals and petals similar, spread-
ing. Lip 3-lobed, provided with a pair of hollow
horn-like calli. Column short, winged; anther ter-
minal; pollinia 4, waxy.
There are only two species, both confined to the
American tropics. One is known from Belize.

arthron (joint) referring to the several-jointed pseu-

weeks. Normal flowers are usually outnumbered by
